summary: Russia and Ukraine agree a prisoner swap but not land, Iran says Hormuz has changed for good, Ebola passes 11,000 cases, and COP31 leaders meet.

question.text: Iran says it and Oman will now oversee the Strait of Hormuz. If shipping companies came to accept that, what might change a few steps later: for other narrow sea lanes, for oil buyers in Asia, and for the treaty rules that govern the sea?

read.title: World leaders to address COP31 as Turkey pushes for new climate deal
read.summary: A clear guide to what COP31 is trying to agree, why Turkey is betting on electrification, and why critics say that is not the same as leaving fossil fuels.

topics.heading: Russia-Ukraine talks in Abu Dhabi end with a prisoner swap deal, but no deal on land
topics.summary: Two days of US-brokered talks ended with Russia and Ukraine agreeing in principle to a large prisoner exchange, with numbers to be set on Thursday.[^1][^2] Both sides say territory is still unresolved, and US envoys head to Moscow and then to Zelenskyy in Dublin.[^1][^3]

lead.title: Abu Dhabi peace talks end with prisoner exchange agreement as US envoys prepare to meet Putin

alsoReported.title: Russia–Ukraine peace talks conclude in Abu Dhabi with prisoner exchange agreement but no breakthrough on territory
Abu Dhabi Talks End With Prisoner Exchange But No Peace Breakthrough

article: The first direct talks between Russia and Ukraine in nine months ended on Wednesday in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates. US envoy Jared Kushner said the two sides had agreed to a prisoner exchange and would settle the numbers the next day.[^1] Zelenskyy had said negotiators discussed 1,000 prisoners from each side, possibly rising to 1,500.[^1] A Ukrainian delegate said it could be one of the largest swaps of the war.[^2]

Both delegations described the swap as the main result. Ukraine's lead negotiator Rustem Umerov said "significant differences remain" on other issues.[^4] Kushner said the hardest question is territory, but reported progress on security guarantees for Ukraine and on ways to monitor a future ceasefire.[^2][^4]

Russia's lead negotiator, Putin aide Vladimir Medinsky, repeated Moscow's demand for land, saying "every inch of our land will be returned to Russia."[^3] Ukraine refuses to give up territory it controls.[^3] Medinsky also said his team did not talk to the European officials who came to Abu Dhabi and questioned why they were there; the US says it wants Europeans in a wider format later.[^1][^4]
The fighting did not pause. Ukraine's prime minister said Russia struck six large electricity substations in central Ukraine during the talks.[^4]

What comes next: Kushner and Steve Witkoff planned to meet Putin in Moscow on Thursday and then Zelenskyy in Dublin.[^1][^3] My read: a big prisoner exchange is likely soon, because both sides have agreed to it before, including a 1,000-for-1,000 swap in May 2025.[^1] A wider deal still depends on the land question, where neither side has moved.
topics.differences: Medinsky frames the talks as being about Europe's whole security system and calls Europe's role unclear.[^2][^3] Kushner and Ukraine frame them as steps toward a ceasefire, with progress on monitoring and guarantees.[^4] A Ukrainian delegate suggested a deal could come "by the New Year"; US negotiators say there is no trust between the sides.[^2]

topics.heading: Iran's top negotiator says Hormuz will 'never return' to how it was before the war
topics.summary: Iran's parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf told Al Jazeera that Iran and Oman have agreed to oversee the Strait of Hormuz, and that Iran awaits a US reply to its seven conditions.[^5] Trump says the US has already won the war.[^6]

lead.title: Hormuz Strait will 'never return' to pre-war status, Iran's Ghalibaf says

alsoReported.title: Nov. 11: Trump claims US has already won the Iran war, now wants 'total victory'

article: Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, the speaker of Iran's parliament and its top negotiator, said in an interview with Al Jazeera published on Wednesday that the Strait of Hormuz will "never return" to its pre-war status.[^5] The strait, between Iran and Oman, normally carries about a fifth of the world's oil and has been largely shut during the eight-month war.

Ghalibaf said Iran and Oman have reached an understanding to oversee the waterway together, as part of a seven-point Iranian plan to end the war.[^5] He argued there are no "free waters" in the strait and that the 1982 UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, the treaty most countries use for shipping rights, does not apply there.[^5] The US is not a party to that treaty, but it has long held that ships have a right to pass through straits like Hormuz.

According to Ghalibaf, Iran sent its conditions to Washington through a Qatari mediator and is waiting for an official answer. Al Jazeera lists them as including an end to the US naval blockade and sanctions, the release of frozen Iranian money, an end to fighting on all fronts and a formal announcement that the war is over. "The ball is now in the American court," he said.[^5]

The US message is different. The Times of Israel reports that President Trump claims the US has already won the war and now wants "total victory".[^6] Ghalibaf, for his part, predicted Trump would face pressure from the new Democratic-led Congress in January.[^5]

My read: both sides are describing the same stalemate in the language of winning. The key test is whether the US answers the Qatari message, and whether shipping companies treat an Iran-Oman arrangement as something they can live with or as a new risk.
topics.differences: Iran, through Ghalibaf, says the strait's rules are now for Iran and Oman to set and that talks need US concessions first.[^5] Trump says the US has already won and wants total victory.[^6] Neither account has been independently confirmed.

topics.heading: Congo's Ebola outbreak passes 11,000 cases, the second largest on record
topics.summary: Government data show 11,042 confirmed Ebola cases and 5,387 deaths in Congo since May, Reuters reports.[^7] The Bundibugyo strain behind it has no approved vaccine or treatment, and cases have reached East, Central and West Africa.[^7][^8]

lead.title: Congo's Ebola cases surpass 11,000, government data show

alsoReported.title: Congo-Kinshasa: Congo Ebola Cases Surpass 11,000 As Death Toll Reaches 5,387

article: Congo's government released figures on Tuesday showing 11,042 confirmed Ebola infections and 5,387 deaths since the outbreak was declared in mid-May.[^7] Reuters says that makes it the second-largest Ebola outbreak on record, behind the 2014 to 2016 West African epidemic, which infected more than 28,600 people.[^7]

Ebola is a virus that causes severe bleeding and organ failure and spreads through contact with the body fluids of sick people. This outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo species, for which there are no approved vaccines or specific treatments.[^7] Vaccine trials are under way, with first results expected in 2027.[^8]

Eight of Congo's 26 provinces are affected, mostly in the east, in Ituri and North Kivu.[^8] Reuters links the spread to late detection, armed conflict and overstretched health services, and many people have died outside treatment centres, which makes tracing harder.[^7] Cases have been reported in Uganda, Kenya and Nigeria, and some patients have been flown to Europe.[^8]

Why it matters: about half of confirmed patients have died.[^8] The World Health Organization's last count, on Nov 3, was 10,668 cases, so the outbreak is still growing by hundreds of cases a week.[^8]

What next: health agencies are asking for more money and supplies.[^8] My read: without a vaccine, slowing this outbreak depends on safe access to the conflict zones in the east, which is the hardest part to change quickly.

topics.heading: Guterres tells COP31 leaders 'the climate crisis is outrunning us'
topics.summary: UN chief Antonio Guterres urged leaders at the COP31 climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, to move away from coal, oil and gas.[^9] Many major leaders stayed away, and Turkey is pushing a plan to raise electricity's share of energy use.[^10][^11]

lead.title: 'Climate crisis is outrunning us,' UN chief Guterres says at COP31

alsoReported.title: World leaders to address COP31 as Turkey pushes for new climate deal
UN chief urges world leaders to tackle fossil fuels at COP31

article: World leaders began two days of speeches at the UN climate conference, COP31, in Antalya, Turkey, on Wednesday. Secretary-General Antonio Guterres opened with a warning: "The brutal truth is that the climate crisis is outrunning us."[^9] He said emissions hit an all-time high in 2025 and accused the fossil fuel industry of delaying action.[^9][^11] This is his last COP before his term ends in December.[^11]

Background: in 2023, countries agreed to "transition away" from fossil fuels, but they have struggled to agree how.[^11] A UN report last month found the world on course to pass 1.5°C of warming, the limit set in the 2015 Paris Agreement.[^10]

The host's main idea is electrification. Turkey proposes a voluntary goal for electricity to supply 35% of the world's energy use by 2035, up from a little over a fifth now.[^10] Critics note the plan does not require that new power be clean.[^10] Brazil, last year's host, has published a road map to cut fossil fuel supply from 2031.[^10]

The guest list says a lot. The US is skipping the talks for a second year, China sent its vice president, and the leaders of France, Germany, Italy, Japan and Canada are not attending.[^9][^11] The EU's climate commissioner said "expectations are not necessarily high."[^11] Iran's president Masoud Pezeshkian is attending and planned to accuse the US and Israel of damaging the environment.[^9]

What next: talks run until Nov 20.[^9] My read: high oil prices from the Iran war make the case for cheaper electricity stronger, but they also make governments nervous about cutting supply, so expect small, voluntary steps rather than a big new deal.

topics.heading: Anthropic sets an IPO price that could value it at $1.4 trillion
topics.summary: AI company Anthropic plans to sell shares at $70 to $78 each, raising up to about $64 billion, with trading expected around Nov 19, TechCrunch reports.[^12] Its filing shows fast-growing revenue and very large losses.[^12]

lead.title: Anthropic sets IPO price range of $70 to $78 per share to reach an implied valuation of $1.404 trillion

article: Anthropic, the company behind the Claude AI models, said in an updated filing on Tuesday that it will offer 825 million shares at $70 to $78 each in its initial public offering (IPO), its first sale of shares to the public.[^12] At the top of the range, that would raise about $64 billion and value the company at about $1.4 trillion.[^12] (A note: Zen Garden is written with Claude, an Anthropic product. This summary sticks to what the filing and reporting say.)

Separately, Anthropic agreed to sell $26 billion of non-voting shares to chip and cloud companies, including Google, Nvidia, Microsoft and TSMC.[^12] Its founders keep a special class of shares with a majority of the votes, so public buyers will have limited say.[^12]

The numbers show the shape of the AI boom. The filing reports $17 billion in revenue in the third quarter, but a net loss of $104 billion over nine months, and about $900 billion in commitments for computing and infrastructure.[^12] The valuation is below the roughly $2 trillion it was reportedly aiming for a few months ago, as markets have become shakier.[^12]

Why it matters: if a company this size lists, ordinary investors and pension funds get direct exposure to frontier AI for the first time at this scale. Shares are expected to trade on Nasdaq around Nov 19, with up to 20% offered to individual investors, according to TechCrunch citing CNBC.[^12]
My read: the IPO will be read as a vote on whether AI's huge spending can turn into profits. A strong debut could encourage more spending; a weak one would add to recent worries about an AI bubble.

topics.heading: US House shelves a vote to impeach Defense Secretary Hegseth, 211 to 204
topics.summary: The Republican-led House voted 211-204 to send Rep. Thomas Massie's impeachment resolution against Pete Hegseth to committee, which effectively ends it for now.[^13] Democrats say they may revive it when they take control in January.[^13]

lead.title: House Sends Hegseth Impeachment Resolution to Judiciary Committee in 211–204 Vote

alsoReported.title: House blocks Massie's effort to impeach Hegseth, voting to kill resolution

article: The US House of Representatives voted 211 to 204 on Tuesday to send a resolution to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to the Judiciary Committee, a move that effectively shelves it.[^14][^13] Impeachment is Congress's way of formally charging an official; a House vote would send the case to a Senate trial.

The resolution was brought by Thomas Massie, a Republican from Kentucky, who was the only Republican to vote against shelving it.[^13] It accuses Hegseth of starting the Iran war without approval from Congress, ignoring laws on civilian casualties, and other actions, including strikes on boats in the Caribbean.[^13] Hegseth called the effort a "farce" and said the charges are "partisan policy disagreements".[^13] President Trump said it "miserably FAILED!"[^13]

Background: only two cabinet secretaries in US history have been impeached, in 1876 and 2024, and neither was removed.[^13] The vote came a week after Democrats won both houses of Congress in the Nov 3 midterms; the new Congress sits in January.[^13]

What next: House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries said "this is not the end of it".[^13] Massie, who retires in January, says he will instead force a vote on a war powers resolution, which would try to limit the president's use of force against Iran.[^13]

My read: this vote shows how much changes in January. The same question could return under a Democratic House, though removing an official still needs two-thirds of the Senate, which neither party has.
topics.differences: Supporters say Hegseth broke the law by waging war without Congress.[^13] Hegseth and Trump say it is a partisan attack on the military, and the White House says the president has authority to direct military operations.[^13][^14]
